name: Listener crossword No 8: A Botanical Crossword

blocks.note: surface reading: any small flower of the countryside
the setter's reading: a particular small lilac-flowered weed of arable fields

explanation.walkthrough: This 1930 botanical puzzle uses plain definitions rather than wordplay; the crossing letters settle which small wild flower is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: Field madder (Sherardia arvensis) is a tiny lilac-flowered annual of arable land, a common British wild flower.

explanation.walkthrough: The entry is the start of ASPARAGUS; this 1930 puzzle fills its short lights with word fragments described this way.
explanation.definitionFit: Asparagus is a garden vegetable grown for its young edible shoots, and its opening trio fills this short light.

blocks.note: surface reading: any scented bush
the setter's reading: the aromatic Mediterranean herb-bush whose oil goes into eau de Cologne

explanation.walkthrough: A plain definition; the crossing letters pick out which perfume shrub is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: Rosemary oil is a classic ingredient of colognes and toilet waters, and the plant is an evergreen shrub.

blocks.note: surface reading: anything you might see on a moor
the setter's reading: the heath plant that carpets moors

explanation.walkthrough: A plain definition of the moorland plant by its habitat.
explanation.definitionFit: Erica is the botanical genus of the heaths, low shrubs that cover acid moorland.

blocks.note: surface reading: any little plant of boggy ground
the setter's reading: the old genus name of marsh purslane

explanation.walkthrough: The genus is ISNARDIA, eight letters in a seven-letter light; the grid drops the final A though the clue as printed does not say so.
explanation.definitionFit: Isnardia palustris, now Ludwigia, is marsh purslane, a small creeping plant of pond margins and marshes.

blocks.note: surface reading: any pot herb grown for cooking
the setter's reading: the lemon-scented mint relative, Melissa

explanation.walkthrough: A plain definition; the crossing letters choose among the many kitchen herbs.
explanation.definitionFit: Lemon balm is a lemon-scented member of the mint family grown in herb beds for teas and cooking.

blocks.note: surface reading: a plant whose blooms resemble cats
the setter's reading: a Latin botanical adjective built from -florus, 'flowered'

explanation.walkthrough: The entry is entirely fixed by its crossing letters except the tenth; the Latin tiara- prefix suggests 'cap-like' rather than the printed 'catlike', so the clue may be misprinted or misread.
explanation.definitionFit: A botanical epithet ending in -florus describes the flowers a plant bears, here likened to a headdress.

the setter's reading: the local Efik word for the ordeal bean, cut to its first three letters

explanation.walkthrough: The native name is ESERE; the calabar bean was used in trial by ordeal in Calabar, Nigeria, and its name gave the drug eserine.
explanation.definitionFit: Esere is the Efik word for the calabar bean, source of the alkaloid eserine, so its first three letters fill the light.

explanation.definitionFit: Kobresia is a genus of small tufted sedges, herbs whose narrow leaves look just like grass.

blocks.note: surface reading: some kind of dye plant
the setter's reading: the West Indian indigo shrub

explanation.walkthrough: A plain definition; this short dye-plant name is a crossword regular.
explanation.definitionFit: Anil is Indigofera suffruticosa, a shrub grown for blue dye; its name comes via Arabic from Sanskrit for dark blue.

blocks.note: surface reading: some common quality of blooms
the setter's reading: a common petal colour

explanation.walkthrough: A plain definition of a colour; the crossing letters choose it from many possible qualities.
explanation.definitionFit: Roses, poppies, tulips and countless other blooms are coloured scarlet or crimson, the commonest bright flower hue.

blocks.note: surface reading: any plant disease
the setter's reading: the drooping of a thirsty or diseased plant

explanation.walkthrough: A plain definition; 'sickness' points to the drooping that marks an ailing plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilt is the limp collapse of leaves and stems, and also the name of several plant diseases that cause it.

clue.text: Half of part of a palm used for a special purpose.

explanation.definitionFit: Raffia is the leaf fibre of the Raphia palm, used for tying and weaving, and its first half fills the light.

blocks.note: surface reading: the common name of a tree
the setter's reading: its botanical genus name

explanation.walkthrough: A plain definition asking for the botanical name behind a common name.

explanation.walkthrough: Beecham's Pills were advertised as 'worth a guinea a box' (a guinea was 21 shillings); the plant meant is the purgative aloe.
explanation.definitionFit: Bitter aloes, the dried juice of aloe leaves, was the chief laxative in Victorian patent pills.

blocks.note: surface reading: bunched like fruit on a vine

explanation.definitionFit: The entry stands for crumpling or crinkling a material, a sense the crossing letters force rather than any common usage.

clue.text: Anagram of a kind of reed.

explanation.walkthrough: The entry is not a word: it is the reed's genus name rearranged so the crossing letters fit.
explanation.definitionFit: Typha is the botanical genus of reedmace, the tall brown-headed reed of ponds often called bulrush.

blocks.note: surface reading: some variety of spud

explanation.walkthrough: The usual spelling is wapato; the grid's five letters, fixed by crossings, drop one A.
explanation.definitionFit: Wapato, the starchy tuber of Sagittaria arrowhead, was called the Indian or duck potato in North America.

explanation.walkthrough: The genus is STYRAX, six letters in a five-letter light; the grid drops the final X though the clue as printed gives no fraction.
explanation.definitionFit: Styrax japonica, the Japanese snowbell, is a species within the storax genus of shrubs and small trees.

blocks.note: surface reading: the stink of rotting vegetation
the setter's reading: the Latin word for a noxious vapour

explanation.walkthrough: A plain definition; the word survives in 'mephitic' and in the skunk genus Mephitis.
explanation.definitionFit: Mephitis was the Roman name for a pestilential vapour rising from the ground, a stench like rotting matter.

definitions.note: the entry lacks the final letter of the genus name

blocks.note: surface reading: any fine-leaved grass
the setter's reading: the genus of silvery hair grasses

explanation.walkthrough: The genus is AIRA, four letters in a three-letter light; the grid drops the final A though the clue as printed gives no fraction.
explanation.definitionFit: Aira is the genus of silvery hair grasses, small annual grasses with very fine, hair-like stems.

explanation.walkthrough: The answer at 48 down is the person behind Aaron's rod, the folk name of great mullein, whose botanical name is Verbascum THAPSUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Thapsus is the botanical epithet of great mullein, the plant commonly called Aaron's rod, and its first syllable fills the light.

clue.text: This King was 'fantastically dressed with wild flowers'.
